opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to understand it is that there are really two different things going on at once, and people tend to conflate them.

If you look at any individual model, think of it as its own little business. You spend some amount on compute to train it, say a year or so before it's deployed, and then over its deployment lifetime it brings in revenue, and the inference has decent margins. If you do the accounting model by model, each one tends to pay back what it cost to train, and then some. So at the level of the unit economics, the business is actually pretty healthy.

What makes it look unprofitable on paper is that at the same time you're deploying that model, you're training the next one, and the next one costs a lot more, maybe several times more. So you have this staircase where today's revenue comes from yesterday's model while today's spending goes to tomorrow's much bigger model. On a cash basis that looks like losing money, but it's more like a company that keeps reinvesting into a factory that's growing very fast.

So spending something like half your compute on research and training isn't a contradiction with being profitable. It's a choice about how much you reinvest versus how much you harvest. If the scaling stopped, if you said "we're not training anything bigger," the business would flip to profitable fairly quickly, because you'd just be serving existing models at a margin. The reason you don't do that is that the frontier keeps moving, and if you stop investing, you fall behind and those margins disappear.

The real risk, and I think about this a lot, isn't the unit economics. It's the forecasting. You have to commit to compute a year or two out, and you're basically betting on how fast demand grows. If revenue grows the way the technology suggests it should, you're fine. If you overbuy compute and the demand curve comes in a bit slower than you predicted, even by a year, that can be really damaging. So a lot of being a responsible business here is not getting caught up in the most optimistic projections. You want to plan so that even if things come in on the more conservative side, you don't go bankrupt. Some players are being more aggressive about that than I'd be comfortable with.

So the short answer: the research spend is basically the cost of staying at the frontier, each model on its own pays for itself, and profitability ultimately comes down to disciplined bets on how fast demand grows, not some fundamental flaw in the model.

r001.rationale: The response says individual models pay back their training costs and discusses demand forecasts, but it does not state that gross margin exceeds 50%.

r002.rationale: It explains that compute commitments for larger future models happen while revenue comes from earlier models, making the business look unprofitable on a cash basis despite healthy model-level economics.

r003.rationale: It identifies forecasting demand incorrectly as a risk: if demand grows more slowly than expected after compute commitments, the business can be seriously harmed.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is that the frame of "half on research" is a little misleading, because it treats research as a cost center that's separate from the product. In this field, the research is the product pipeline. The model you train this year is what you sell next year, and the capability jump between generations is large enough that the next model basically obsoletes the last one. So if you stop spending on research, you don't become a more profitable company, you become a company that's selling last year's model into a market where someone else is selling this year's.

The way I like to describe it is that each model is kind of its own business. You spend a large amount of money to train it, and then over the following year or two it generates revenue that, so far at least, has substantially exceeded what it cost to train. The problem is that at the same time that model is paying for itself, you're spending an even larger amount training the next one. So if you look at the company's books in any given year, it looks like you're losing money, when actually every individual model is quite profitable. It's just that the capital expenditure is growing exponentially while the returns lag by a year or two.

Now, that only works as long as a couple of things remain true. One is that the scaling trend continues, that each generation is actually a big enough improvement that people will pay for it. I think the evidence is pretty strong that this is continuing. The second is that there's enough demand to absorb the increased capability, and what we've seen, especially on the enterprise side and in coding, is that demand has been growing faster than almost anyone expected. Revenue has gone up something like an order of magnitude a year for a few years running.

The last piece, which I'd say is specific to how we've structured things, is that we try not to overinvest in inference capacity that we're not using. Research compute is productive on day one. Idle inference compute is just a loss. So the question isn't really "how do you spend half your compute on research and make money," it's "how do you get the ratio right so that you're training the models the market wants and serving them to the people who want them." At some point the exponential has to flatten out, and at that point you'd expect the research fraction to come down and the business to look much more conventionally profitable. But I don't think we're anywhere close to that yet, and I think the companies that pull back early are going to regret it.

r001.rationale: The response says each model has so far generated more revenue than it cost to train and discusses demand, but it does not state that gross margin exceeds 50% or connect profitability to correctly predicting demand.

r002.rationale: It notes that unused inference capacity is a loss and that rising research spending can make the company’s books look unprofitable. It does not clearly identify building compute capacity ahead of demand as what obscures underlying profitability.

r003.rationale: The response discusses demand growth and the need for enough demand, but does not identify demand prediction errors as obscuring underlying profitability.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the key distinction is between the margins on serving the models and how much you’re choosing to invest in the next generation. You can have a healthy business selling access to a model and still spend a huge fraction of your overall compute budget on research. That research spending can make the company unprofitable today, but it doesn’t necessarily mean the underlying product is uneconomic.

Now, the investment does have to pay off. You’re betting that better models will be useful for more things, that people will pay for those capabilities, and that you can serve them efficiently enough to earn a return. If every generation costs dramatically more to develop without creating correspondingly more value, then that doesn’t work.

So I wouldn’t say, “Research is an investment, therefore we can ignore it.” Ultimately, revenue has to cover research too. The question is whether you’re looking at a business that’s structurally losing money or one that’s reinvesting aggressively because the opportunity is growing. Spending half your compute on research, by itself, doesn’t tell you which one you have.

r001.rationale: The response says model sales can support heavy research spending and that revenue must cover research, but it does not state the gross margin must exceed 50% or that profitability depends on predicting demand correctly.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify building compute capacity ahead of demand as something that can obscure the business model’s profitability.

r003.rationale: It discusses betting that customers will pay for better models, but does not say demand prediction errors can obscure the underlying profitability of the business model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that spending half your compute on research doesn’t mean you’re spending half your revenue on research. It depends on the margins you earn on the other half—the compute you use to serve customers.

If customers get enough value from the models, you can charge more than it costs to run them, and that surplus can fund research. Whether it actually does is a quantitative question: how much demand is there, what does serving that demand cost, and how quickly are those costs falling?

The complication is growth. You’re paying for research today that might produce revenue later, and if you keep increasing the scale of that research, you can have a valuable business that still consumes cash. So I’d distinguish the question of whether serving models is profitable from whether the whole company is profitable while making those investments. The first can be true well before the second.

r001.rationale: The response says customer-serving margins can fund research, but it does not state that gross margin must exceed 50% or that profitability depends on predicting demand correctly.

r002.rationale: It discusses research investments and growth consuming cash, but does not identify building compute capacity ahead of demand as obscuring the business model’s underlying profitability.

r003.rationale: It asks how much demand there is, but does not identify demand prediction errors as obscuring underlying profitability.
